Definition: The country's total international internet bandwidth capacity per internet user, indicating the quality and capacity of the country's connection to the global internet. Determined by submarine cable landings (for coastal states), cross-border terrestrial fibre (for landlocked states), and satellite links.
redteam_note: No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Fetched the originally cited Research ICT Solutions (2021) report, which records used international bandwidth of 9.40 Mbps per 10,000 population in 2019 (equivalent to under 1 kbit/s per capita, and still well under 5 kbit/s once divided among the smaller internet-using population). A second, independent source (the mAccess Diagnostic Tool / digitaldevelopment.org country profile) separately estimates international bandwidth per user at 0.77 kbit/s. Both corroborate the 'Very Low (<5 kbit/s)' rating. No more recent ITU country-specific figure could be confirmed via ITU DataHub (interactive tool, no static figure retrievable). Score of 1 confirmed unchanged.
revised_comments: DR Congo's connection to the global internet remains very thin relative to its internet-using population. Research ICT Solutions estimated used international bandwidth at around 9.4 Mbps per 10,000 population in 2019, equivalent to well under 1 kbit/s per capita, while a separate mAccess Diagnostic Tool estimate puts international bandwidth per internet user at around 0.77 kbit/s. Both figures sit far below the 5 kbit/s per user threshold, reflecting DRC's limited submarine cable landings and cross-border fibre capacity relative to demand.

Definition: Whether the country has enacted legal or regulatory requirements mandating that certain categories of data (personal data, government data, financial data, or critical infrastructure data) be stored within national borders. Central to data sovereignty debates in Africa.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Originally scored 0/Unknown with no source. A light check surfaced clear evidence of the DRC's Digital Code Law (Ordonnance-loi N°23-010 of 13 March 2023, published in the official journal 11 April 2023), fetched and read via DLA Piper's Data Protection Laws of the World (last modified 4 February 2026) and the official gazetted law text. The Code establishes a Data Protection Authority (Autorité de Protection des Données, APD) and restricts transfer of personal data abroad, permitting it only where the receiving country/organisation offers protection equal to or better than that guaranteed under the Code. This is a general, economy-wide condition on personal data broadly rather than a strict mandate to store data within national borders, and DLA Piper notes the APD has not yet been established, so the declaration/authorisation regimes are 'not yet in practice complied with'. Recalculated to 4 (comprehensive requirements for personal data or broad categories) rather than 5, reflecting the enacted but not-yet-enforced status. Flagged for human review because classifying an adequacy-style cross-border transfer restriction as 'data localisation' (as opposed to a distinct transfer-restriction category) is open to interpretation depending on tracker methodology, and because enforcement is not yet operational.
revised_comments: The Democratic Republic of Congo's Digital Code Law (Ordonnance-loi N°23-010 of 13 March 2023) establishes a legal framework for personal data protection, including a national Data Protection Authority (Autorité de Protection des Données). It restricts transfer of personal data to other countries, permitting this only where the receiving jurisdiction or organisation provides data protection equal to or better than that guaranteed domestically. This constitutes a comprehensive, economy-wide requirement applying to personal data broadly rather than a narrow sectoral rule. Implementing decrees and the Data Protection Authority itself have not yet been fully operationalised, so practical enforcement of the declaration and authorisation regimes remains limited.

Definition: Affordability of electricity for residential and small business consumers, measured as cost of electricity relative to income levels. High electricity costs are a direct barrier to ICT adoption and data center viability.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Originally scored 0/Unknown with no source. A light check surfaced substantive tariff data going beyond a simple confirmation, so the row was escalated to a fuller check. DRC's residential low-voltage electricity tariffs have been fixed by ministerial decree since 2009 (confirmed still unchanged in USD terms by government statements reported June 2024) at roughly USD 0.027–0.087/kWh depending on customer category, and GlobalPetrolPrices.com (September 2025) separately records an average residential price of USD 0.074/kWh. GNI per capita (World Bank Atlas method, via Macrotrends) was approximately USD 680 in 2023 (about USD 56.7/month). Assuming an indicative basic monthly household consumption of 30–50 kWh, the electricity cost works out to roughly 3.9%–6.5% of monthly income, straddling the 'Moderate (3–5%)' and 'Expensive (6–10%)' bands on the defined scale. No authoritative source computes this affordability ratio directly for DR Congo — it is a back-of-envelope estimate from separate tariff and income figures, not a reported statistic — so the code is kept at 0/Unknown rather than guessed, and the row is flagged for human review with the underlying data provided so a reviewer can finalise a code once a basic-consumption benchmark is agreed.
revised_comments: Residential electricity tariffs in DR Congo have been fixed by ministerial decree since 2009, last confirmed unchanged in USD terms in mid-2024, at roughly USD 0.027–0.087 per kWh for low-voltage residential customers depending on category; GlobalPetrolPrices.com records an average residential price of USD 0.074 per kWh as of September 2025. Against a GNI per capita of around USD 680 (2023), a typical basic household bill represents a moderate-to-high share of monthly income, though no primary source publishes a specific affordability ratio for the country, so overall affordability cannot yet be confidently classified on the defined scale.
